title: Semantic Versioning (SemVer) Explained
description: How MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH version numbers work, what each part signals, and how npm's caret and tilde ranges interpret them.
bodyHtml:
Semantic Versioning uses a three-part number: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, e.g. 2.5.1. Each part means something specific about compatibility, not just "how much changed."

PartIncrement whenExample
MAJORYou make a breaking, backward-incompatible change1.x.x → 2.0.0
MINORYou add functionality that's backward-compatible2.4.x → 2.5.0
PATCHYou make a backward-compatible bug fix2.5.0 → 2.5.1

When MAJOR increments, MINOR and PATCH reset to 0. When MINOR increments, PATCH resets to 0.

npm range operators

RangeMeansAllows
^2.5.1Compatible with 2.5.1Any 2.x.x ≥ 2.5.1, but not 3.0.0
~2.5.1Approximately 2.5.1Any 2.5.x ≥ 2.5.1, but not 2.6.0
2.5.1Exact versionOnly 2.5.1
*Any versionAnything

Caret (^) is the npm default and the loosest common choice — it allows new features and fixes but blocks breaking changes. Tilde (~) is stricter, allowing only patch-level updates.

Pre-1.0 versions

Under SemVer, 0.x.y means "anything can change at any time" — there's no stability guarantee. Some tools treat ^0.5.1 as equivalent to ~0.5.1 for this reason: with major version 0, npm treats the MINOR digit as the breaking-change boundary instead.
